newsitem.title: USA: Indian pleads no contest to spying charges in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Indian pleads no contest to spying charges in U.S.

text.p: A businessman from India pleaded no contest on Monday to a charge of espionage and was sentenced to the 15 months he had already spent in a U.S. prison.

The only comment Aluru Prasad, 50, of Hyderabad, India, made following the brief hearing was to say that he planned to return to his country on Wednesday. He entered the no contest plea to one count of trying to spy.

Prasad was indicted in October 1995 on charges he had attempted to obtain classified information, including details about a special paint used in making the Stealth bomber invisible to radar, with the intention of selling that information to the former Soviet Union.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Alexandra Leake told U.S. District Judge Reginald Lindsay that "in view of the government's decision and recent events it is no longer in the national interest to prosecute Mr. Prasad."
Sources close to the case said the government's plan to fully prosecute Prasad was crippled because it lost access to a key witness against Prasad.

The sources said the U.S. Justice Department was planning to use the testimony of retired KGB agent Vladimir Galkin against Prasad. But Galkin, whose Oct. 29 arrest in New York prompted outrage from Moscow as well as the State Department and the Central Intelligence Agency, was released.

Prasad, a graduate of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Sloan School of Management and a self-made millionaire with a battery factory in Hyderabad, was tried over the summer of attempting to obtain military secrets and selling them to the KGB.
But Lindsay declared a mistrial in August, ruling that the jury had heard evidence that would unfairly prejudice their verdict.
